blocks.text: Moreover, just as these locusts had been brought into Egypt by the קדים Kadim wind, that is, the east wind, so they were carried away by the ים wind, the wind of the sea, that is, the west wind, and cast into the Red Sea. For that locusts are carried by the wind is commonplace. Pliny, in the place cited above: "There is also another way in which they perish. Lifted up in swarms by the wind, they fall into seas or pools." Jerome on Joel ch. 2: "In our own times too we have seen swarms of locusts cover the land of Judaea: which afterwards, by the mercy of the Lord, etc., when a wind arose, were hurled into the first and the last sea." Orosius, book 4, ch. 11, on the African locusts: "Seized by a sudden wind, and driven together into masses, and carried for a long time through the air, they were plunged into the African sea" ^{(6)}. But the קדים Kadim wind, which brought the locusts into Egypt, although properly it means the east wind, is nevertheless also taken for the south wind, as we proved ^{b)} in the chapter On the Miracle of the Quails. Thus the Greek translators render it Νότον [Noton] and Λίβα [Liba], that is, Notus and Africus, and καύσωνα [kausōna], the burning wind. And perhaps it will not be beside the point to interpret it so here: since the east wind could have brought locusts into Egypt only from Arabia, but the south wind from Ethiopia, which is far more fertile in this pest. Accordingly الحبشان [al-ḥbshān] alhabsan, a kind of locust, takes its name [III, 288] from the Abaseni, or Abyssinians, in whose soil it is born. And in Ethiopia some peoples lived on locusts alone, which the winds, partly westerly, partly southerly, carried there in an almost incredible abundance. And this around the spring equinox, the very time of year at which they were brought into Egypt. Agatharchides, where he speaks of the Acridophagi: Ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν ἐαρινὴν ἰσημερίαν, ὅτε Λίβες παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς καὶ Ζέφυροι πνέουσι παμμεγέθεις, ἀκρίδων πλῆθος ἀμύθητον ἐκ τῆς ἀνιστορήτου μετὰ τῶν ἀνέμων παραγίνεται χώρας [Hypo de tēn earinēn isēmerian, hote Libes par᾽ autois kai Zephyroi pneousi pammegetheis, akridōn plēthos amythēton ek tēs anistorētou meta tōn anemōn paraginetai chōras]. And Diodorus, book 3: Κατὰ γὰρ τὴν ἐαρινὴν ὥραν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς Ζέφυροι καὶ Λίβες παμμεγέθεις ἐκρίπτουσιν ἐκ τῆς ἐρήμου πλῆθος ἀκρίδων ἀμύθητον [Kata gar tēn earinēn hōran par᾽ autois Zephyroi kai Libes pammegetheis ekriptousin ek tēs erēmou plēthos akridōn amythēton]. And Strabo, book 16: Ζῶσι δ᾽ ἀπὸ ἀκρίδων, ἃς οἱ ἐαρινοὶ Λίβες, καὶ Ζέφυροι, πνέοντες μεγάλοι, συνελαύνουσιν εἰς τοὺς τόπους τούτους [Zōsi d᾽ apo akridōn, has hoi earinoi Libes, kai Zephyroi, pneontes megaloi, synelaunousin eis tous topous toutous]. Accordingly these same winds seem to have brought the locusts into Egypt from the same places, that is, from Ethiopia ^{(7)}. For as to the view of most, that they were created by God, they will hardly persuade me of it; because Scripture relates nothing of the kind, but says that they were brought by a wind which blew all day and all night. Nor are miracles to be invented without necessity. None such appears here, since more locusts are produced in Ethiopia, near Egypt, than in any part of the world. The miracle, therefore, lay not in God's producing so prodigious a multitude of locusts, but in his bringing it at his nod. And in that the same God who had brought them, at the prayer of Moses, his servant, [col. 464] immediately took them away, raising another wind, namely the west wind, which the Hebrews call רוח ים, the wind of the sea, because they have the sea to the west. And as that wind blew with great force, all the locusts were cast into the Red Sea, not even one being left in all the borders of Egypt. For since the Red Sea lies to the east of Egypt, they had to be driven there by a west wind.
